title: A year of selling, read in order
subtitle: What the sample dataset says about 2020, and what it refuses to say
standfirst: This is the demonstration dataset — one company, two products, four customers, a year of daily orders. It is small enough to check by hand, which makes it a good place to see what a narrative does.
Every figure below is computed from the data loaded right now. Change the period at the top and the sentences change with it. Every claim carries a check, and the checks are allowed to fail.

chapters.title: The year in three numbers

figures.label: Gross margin
figures.note: Revenue less the cost of what was sold

prose: Across the loaded period the company billed {{revenue}} and kept {{margin}} of it as gross margin, on {{units}} units shipped.
Those three numbers are the whole business in outline. Everything that follows is an attempt to say where they came from — because a total tells you the size of something, never its shape.
chapters.takeaway: Start with the totals, then refuse to stop there.

chapters.title: Revenue and margin do not move together
prose: Plot the two against each other and the gap opens up. The best day returned {{best}}; the worst returned {{worst}}.

A negative worst day is not a rounding artefact: it is a day that cost more to serve than it billed. A day can be busy and unprofitable, and that is the first thing a revenue chart alone will never tell you.
chapters.takeaway: Busy is not the same as profitable, and the difference is a daily fact, not an annual one.

checks.label: Every day returned a positive margin
Revenue is at least the margin it produced

chapters.title: Price is the lever
prose: The average unit went out at {{price}} against {{cost}} to buy. The distance between those two is the entire margin, and it is set before a single order is taken.
Volume moves the total. Price moves the rate. Confusing the two is how a company sells more and earns less.

On the days where that gap closed entirely, the order shipped below cost and the day ran at a loss. The check below counts them and names the dates — a handful out of the whole period, which is exactly the kind of thing a monthly total hides.
chapters.takeaway: Volume changes the size of the business; price changes whether it works — and a few days a year, it did not.

checks.label: The average price stayed above the average cost

chapters.title: Where the year actually went
prose: Read cumulatively rather than daily and the noise drops out: {{cumRevenue}} banked, {{cumMargin}} of it kept.

A cumulative line only ever rises, which makes it flattering and easy to read badly. What it is good for is slope — where the line steepens, something changed, and that is the date worth asking about.
chapters.takeaway: Look at the slope, not the height.
